name: Phytate (inositol hexaphosphate)
short: Dietary phytate strongly inhibits iron absorption; a review links it to iron deficiency in infants on cereal and legume foods. It also lowers zinc absorption. No supplement-trial safety data found.
text: The cited evidence concerns phytate eaten in foods, not phytate supplements; no adverse-event data from trials of phytate supplements taken by mouth were found in the cited sources. A review describes phytic acid as a potent inhibitor of iron absorption and states that low iron absorption from cereal- and legume-based complementary foods is a major factor in iron deficiency in infants. A 2024 review states that phytate binds avidly to, and can reduce gastrointestinal absorption of, phosphate and many minerals and trace elements including iron, zinc, calcium and magnesium, and that the human intestine lacks the enzyme that breaks phytate down. A review of human studies concluded that detrimental effects of phytate on zinc bioavailability could be demonstrated, although the studies were not designed to show whether interactions seen in animals also apply to humans. On the other side, a review of legumes states that in a balanced diet containing animal protein a high intake of legumes is not considered a risk for mineral supply. The 2024 review also reports that, in trials in haemodialysis patients, phytate given intravenously (a different route) may decrease vascular calcification; its abstract does not describe adverse effects. No data on interactions with medicines were found in the cited sources.
